## What is a Regular Expression? {.section-card}

A **regular expression** (also called *regex*) is a sequence of characters that defines a search pattern. They are used to match and manipulate text.

::: {.key-idea}
**Common uses:**
- Cleaning messy data (removing symbols, fixing formats)
- Extracting structured info from text (emails, dates, phone numbers)
- Feature engineering (hashtags, mentions, sentiment cues)
- Web scraping and log parsing
- Data validation for preprocessing pipelines
:::

## Examples {.section-card}

::: {.demo-box}
- `[a-z]+` — matches any sequence of one or more lowercase letters
- `\d{3}-\d{2}-\d{4}` — matches a number (e.g., SSN) in format `123-45-6789`
- `^https?://` — matches beginning of a URL (`http` or `https`)
- `[aeiouyAEIOUY]` — matches any vowel (and `y`)
:::

## Syntax of Regular Expressions {.section-card}

| Component | Role |
|---|---|
| **Characters** | A sequence of symbols that define a search pattern |
| **Metacharacters** | Characters with specific meaning |
| **Character classes** | Groups that can match any one of a set |
| **Quantifiers** | Specify number of occurrences |
| **Anchors** | Match the position |
| **Alternation** | The "or" operator |

## Metacharacters {.section-card}

| Char | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `[]` | Character classes |
| `\` | Escapes metacharacters / specifies special sequences |
| `{}` | Quantifier — number of repeats |
| `*` | Zero or more |
| `+` | One or more |
| `?` | Zero or one |
| `^` | Start of pattern OR complement in a class |
| `$` | End of pattern |
| `.` | Any character except newline |
| `\|` | Alternation (or) |
| `()` | Groups |

## Character Classes {.section-card}

Specified using `[ ]` — groups of characters that satisfy the search.

::: {.key-idea}
**Ranges:** `[a-zA-Z]` matches any letter. Metacharacters (except `\`) are **not active** inside classes, so `[akm$]` matches `"a"`, `"k"`, `"m"`, `"$"`.

If `^` is the **first character** in a class, it means **complement**: `[^aeiou]` matches anything except lowercase vowels.
:::

## The Backslash `\` {.section-card}

::: {.key-idea}
The backslash `\` signals special sequences and is used to escape metacharacters.

It can even escape itself: `\\` searches for `\`.
:::

## Some Special Sequences {.section-card}

| Seq | Meaning | Pattern | Example match |
|---|---|---|---|
| `\d` | A digit | `file_\d\d` | `file 21` |
| `\w` | Alphanumeric | `\w-\w\w\w` | `A-b23` |
| `\s` | White space | `a\sb\sc` | `a b c` |
| `\D` | A non-digit | `\D\D\D` | `abc` |
| `\W` | Non-alphanumeric | `\W\W\W\W\W` | `*-+=)` |
| `\S` | Non-whitespace | `\S\S` | `Hi` |

## Quantifiers {.section-card}

| Quant | Meaning | Pattern | Example match |
|---|---|---|---|
| `+` | One or more times | `\w-\w+` | `A-bbb32` |
| `{d}` | Exactly d times | `\D{3}` | `Abc` or `)))` |
| `{d1,d2}` | d1 to d2 times | `\d{2,4}` | `12` or `345` |
| `{d,}` | d or more times | `\w{3,}` | `Anything` |
| `*` | Zero or more times | `A*B*C*` | `AAACCC` |
| `?` | One or zero times | `colou?r` | `color` or `colour` |

## Anchors {.section-card}

| Anchor | Meaning | Pattern | Matches / Not |
|---|---|---|---|
| `^` | Start of string | `^Hello` | "Hello world" ✓, "Say Hello" ✗ |
| `$` | End of string | `world$` | "Hello world" ✓, "worldwide" ✗ |
| `\b` | Word boundary | `\bcat\b` | "cat" ✓, "concatenate" ✗ |
| `\B` | Non-word boundary | `\Bcat\B` | "concatenate" ✓, "cat" ✗ |

## Anchors, continued {.section-card}

::: {.key-idea}
- `\A` — matches only at the **start** of string
- `\Z` — matches only at the **end** of string
- `\b` — word boundary
:::

::: {.warning-box}
`\b` can interfere with Python's string literals. Use **raw string literals** with `r`, e.g., `r"\d+.\d?"`.
:::

## Read & Decipher (Simple) {.exercise-slide}

What does each regex do? What would it match?

1. `\bcat\b`
2. `\b\d{5}\b`
3. `^[A-Z][a-z]+$`

::: {.exercise-check}
Hints and solutions on the next slides.
:::

## Read & Decipher (Simple) — Hints {.exercise-slide}

::: {.key-idea}
Think about what each piece means:
- `\b` = word boundary
- `\d{5}` = exactly five digits
- `^[A-Z]` = starts with an uppercase letter
- `[a-z]+` = one or more lowercase letters
- `$` = end of string
:::

## Read & Decipher (Simple) — Solutions {.exercise-slide}

1. `\bcat\b` — matches the **whole word** `cat`
2. `\b\d{5}\b` — matches a **5-digit token** (US ZIP code)
3. `^[A-Z][a-z]+$` — matches a **capitalized word** (e.g., `Kerby`)

::: {.exercise-check}
All three target different kinds of "words" in text.
:::

## Read & Decipher (Medium) {.exercise-slide}

What does each regex do? What would it match?

1. `^\s*\#.*$`
2. `https?://[^\s)]+`

::: {.exercise-check}
Hints and solution on the next slide.
:::

## Read & Decipher (Medium) — Solutions {.exercise-slide}

::: {.key-idea}
1. `^\s*\#.*$` — matches **comment lines** (optional leading spaces, a `#`, then anything to end of line)
2. `https?://[^\s)]+` — matches a **simple URL** starting with `http` or `https`, continuing until a space or `)`.
:::

## How Would You Extract Phone Numbers? {.exercise-slide}

**Task:** Find all U.S. phone numbers `123-456-7890` in text.

::: {.key-idea}
**Hints:** `\d` means digit, `{n}` means exactly n times.
:::

::: {.exercise-check}
Solution on the next slide.
:::

## Extract Phone Numbers — Solution {.demo-slide}

::: {.demo-box}
```python
import re

text = "Call 801-555-1234 or 212-999-8888 today!"
pattern = r"\b\d{3}-\d{3}-\d{4}\b"
print(re.findall(pattern, text))
# ['801-555-1234', '212-999-8888']
```
:::

::: {.tip-box}
The `\b` anchors ensure we don't grab digits embedded in longer numbers.
:::

## How Would You Extract Email Addresses? {.exercise-slide}

**Task:** Identify all email addresses in text.

::: {.key-idea}
**Hints:** Start with word characters before `@`, match the domain, use `+` for one or more.
:::

::: {.exercise-check}
Solution on the next slide.
:::

## Extract Email Addresses — Solution {.demo-slide}

::: {.demo-box}
```python
import re

text = "Contact us at help@university.edu"
pattern = r"\b\w+@\w+\.\w+\b"
print(re.findall(pattern, text))
# ['help@university.edu']
```
:::

::: {.tip-box}
`\w+` matches one or more word characters — the local part and the domain.
:::

## Python `re` Library — Matching {.section-card}

| Function | Returns |
|---|---|
| `re.findall(pattern, string)` | All matching substrings as a list |
| `re.match(pattern, string)` | Matches at the **beginning** of the string |
| `re.search(pattern, string)` | Finds the **first** match anywhere |
| `re.finditer(pattern, string)` | Iterator of match objects |
| `re.compile(pattern)` | Compiles a pattern for repeated use |

## Python `re` Library — Modifying Strings {.section-card}

| Function | Description |
|---|---|
| `re.split(pattern, string)` | Splits the string where the RE matches |
| `re.sub(pattern, replace, string)` | Replaces matches with `replace` |
| `re.subn(pattern, replace, string)` | Same as `sub`, but returns a `(result, count)` tuple |

## `re` Isn't Always Necessary {.section-card}

::: {.key-idea}
Python's built-in string methods often do the job:

`.endswith()` · `.startswith()` · `.join()` · `.find()` · `.replace()` · `.strip()` · `.rstrip()` · `.lstrip()` · `.strip('#')` · `.split()` · `.lower()` · `.upper()`
:::

## Applying to Pandas {.section-card}

::: {.key-idea}
- Use the **`.str`** attribute for vectorized string operations.
- Use the **`.apply()`** method with a lambda function for regex-powered logic.
:::

## Pandas Example {.demo-slide}

::: {.demo-box}
```python
import pandas as pd
import re

data = {'text': ["Hello, World!",
                 "The rain in Spain",
                 "How are you?"]}
df = pd.DataFrame(data)

df['uppercase_text'] = df['text'].str.upper()
df['words_starting_with_S'] = df['text'].apply(
    lambda x: re.findall(r'\bS\w+', x)
)
```
:::

::: {.tip-box}
`.str.upper()` needs no regex; `.apply()` with `re.findall` unlocks pattern power.
:::

::: notes
- This deck introduces regular expressions as a text-processing tool for data cleaning and feature engineering.
- Emphasize the layered structure: characters → metacharacters → classes → quantifiers → anchors → alternation.
- The two "Read & Decipher" exercises build intuition before students write their own patterns.
- Phone-number and email-extraction exercises bridge from reading regex to writing Python code with `re`.
- Remind students that simple string methods often suffice — regex shines when structure varies.
- Pandas integration shows how regex scales to real dataframes via `.str` and `.apply()`.
- The "raw string" tip matters: Python's `\b` becomes a backspace unless prefixed with `r`.
:::
